lesson.title: The Night the Wall Came Down: November 9, 1989
lesson.summary: On the night of November 9, 1989, confused East German border guards opened the checkpoints in the Berlin Wall, and jubilant crowds tore down the concrete barrier that had divided the city, and the world, for nearly three decades.
lesson.body:
East Germany had built the Berlin Wall in August 1961 to stop the flow of its citizens escaping to the West through Berlin, and for nearly three decades the wall stood as the most visible symbol of the Cold War's division of Europe. By 1989, the reforms Gorbachev had introduced in the Soviet Union, and his signal that Moscow would not intervene militarily to save communist governments in Eastern Europe, gave reform movements across the region room to grow that they had never had before.

The changes came quickly across Eastern Europe in 1989. In Poland, the independent trade union Solidarity, led by Lech Walesa, won a landslide victory in partly free elections in June 1989, the first real crack in communist rule in the region. In Hungary, the government opened its border with Austria that summer, and thousands of East Germans began traveling to Hungary and then on to the West, exploiting the new gap in the Iron Curtain. Inside East Germany itself, growing numbers of citizens joined weekly protests, especially the Monday demonstrations in Leipzig, demanding freedom to travel and political reform.

The wall's fall itself came almost by accident. On the evening of November 9, 1989, an East German government spokesman, Gunter Schabowski, announced at a press conference that new, looser travel regulations would apply, and when asked when they would take effect, he mistakenly said immediately, without realizing the actual plan called for a more gradual, orderly process. As news spread, thousands of East Berliners gathered at the wall's checkpoints demanding to cross, and overwhelmed and confused border guards, with no clear orders to stop them, opened the gates that night. Crowds of East and West Berliners climbed onto the wall itself in celebration, and in the days that followed, people began breaking off pieces of the concrete barrier with hammers and chisels.

The fall of the Berlin Wall did not immediately reunify Germany, but it made reunification nearly unstoppable, and Germany formally reunited as a single country on October 3, 1990, less than a year later. The image of the wall coming down became the defining symbol of communism's collapse in Eastern Europe, a peaceful revolution rooted directly in the space that Gorbachev's glasnost and his retreat from earlier Soviet policies of military intervention had opened up.
